_readme: SOURCE DEFECTS in the chapterwise compilation, found in Phase 0 and adjudicated
against the raw board papers where those are readable.
THE RULE THAT DECIDED EVERY ENTRY: a defect report is a HYPOTHESIS ABOUT WHOSE
DEFECT IT IS, and only the printed paper settles it. Two findings here looked like
compilation errors and turned out to be the BOARD's own misprints, faithfully
transcribed (see `boardDefects`). One looked fine and turned out to be the
compilation silently CORRECTING the board (see `compilationDivergesFromPaper`).
Do not fix any of these from arithmetic alone.
PAPER READABILITY — this is what makes a defect cheap or expensive to settle:
March 2022, March 2023  → text layer, readable directly (5,652 / 6,826 chars)
2015-2020, 2024, 2025   → SCANNED, 0-88 chars of text. Need render + vision.
NOTHING HERE IS FIXED YET. This file is the work list for the repair pass; a
question whose defect cannot be settled from its own paper is SKIPPED, not guessed.
REPAIR IS PER-CHAPTER, not one big pass. Each chapter's ingest settles its own
entries below before committing, because a scanned paper has to be located, cropped
and read one block at a time. Recipe that worked (see the logic-12-pyq#5 entry):
render the page with PyMuPDF at ~110 dpi clipped to a fraction of page height —
the full page at 170 dpi is 4217x6201 and too large to read in one go.
A STEM CAN BE WRONG EVEN WHEN THE OPTIONS ARE MISSING, and the options are often
what proves it — logic-12-pyq#5 turned out to have a misread symbol in the stem that
would have shipped a question whose correct answer was not among its own options.
When recovering options, re-read the stem too.
⚠ NEVER CALL TWO OPTIONS DUPLICATES FROM FLATTENED TEXT. A PDF text layer (and
pandoc's output) strips fraction structure, so \dfrac{4-\pi}{2} and 4-\dfrac{\pi}{2}
BOTH flatten to '4 - \pi 2' and read as identical — while being 0.4292 and 2.4292.
This produced a false duplicate-option report during the sibling textbook ingest on
2026-08-12, refuted only by re-reading the page at 3x zoom. A duplicate-option claim
is only sound from the rendered page or from structured LaTeX, never from flat text.

_finding: 18 questions are multiple-choice in the printed paper but reach us without a full
(a)-(d) option set. After the cross-chapter duplicate drops, 16 distinct questions
need repair.
HOW THEY WERE FOUND, because the first count was badly wrong. An initial probe
looked for a literal 'Options:' label and found FIVE. That label is only present
when the compilation started an option list and lost it; ten more questions dropped
the label too and therefore read as ordinary subjective questions. The reliable
signals are structural, not textual:
Q1-block       Q.1 IS the multiple-choice block — the 2022 and 2023 papers state
this in their own printed instructions ('Q. 1 contains Eight
multiple choice type of questions'). Q.1(B) in the pre-2022
pattern is short-answer and is excluded.
colon-artifact a stem ending in a bare '\:' is where the option list was stripped.
Confirmed: 'The maximum value of f(x) = log x / x is \:' is printed
in the 2022 paper with four options.
A THIRD signal was tried and REJECTED: 'tagged Q.n(A) for n>=2'. It fired on 20
questions and is simply wrong — in the pre-2022 pattern Q.n(A) is the first
sub-part of question n, not a choice block. It swept in 'Discuss the statement
pattern, using truth table', 'prove that tan(theta) = ...' and 'Find the
probability ...'. Do not reinstate it.

stemFix.from: The dual of statement \(r \vee (p \vee q)\) is __________.
stemFix.to: The dual of statement \(t \vee (p \vee q)\) is __________.
stemFix.why: The compilation misread the printed italic 't' as 'r'. The OPTION SET proves it: options (a)/(b) begin with 'c' (contradiction) and (c)/(d) with 't' (tautology), and duality swaps t <-> c. If the stem really were a propositional variable r, the correct dual would be 'r AND (p AND q)', which appears in none of the four options. A scanned italic serif t is easily read as r at low resolution.
stemFix.consequence: Answer is (b) c AND (p AND q). Ingesting the compilation's 'r' would have shipped a question whose correct answer is not among its own options.

_finding: A question can arrive with a FULL (a)-(d) option set and still be broken —
the compilation mis-copied an option. This is invisible to every structural
probe (four options, one key, no duplicates) and shows up only when the
question is actually SOLVED and no option matches.
FOUND 2026-08-13 while blind-deriving the pilot chapter's five MCQ keys: two
of the five (#1, #3) had NO correct option. Both are the same question — 'the
negation of p ^ (q -> r)' — set in March 2016 and again in March 2022, which
is what made the pattern visible. Source-verifying both settled them in
OPPOSITE directions, which is the point: an arithmetic dead end does not say
whose fault it is.
#1 (March 2016) → OURS. The compilation corrupted TWO options.
#3 (March 2022) → the BOARD's. The paper prints it exactly as we have it.
So a no-correct-option result is a HYPOTHESIS, never a verdict. Read the page.

fixes.why: The paper's (D) IS the correct negation, ~p or (q and ~r). The compilation wrote its outer 'or' as 'and', which deleted the answer from the question; it made the same or->and slip in (A). Two independent slips of the same kind in one option block.
fixes.consequence: Without this repair the question ships unanswerable. The key is D.

_finding: The compilation embeds the board's switching-circuit DIAGRAMS as images and
ALSO writes its own prose description of each one in the stem, e.g. '(Circuit
diagram depicting S1 and S2 in parallel, connected to S3 in series)'.
All four descriptions were compared against the extracted PNGs on 2026-08-13.
NONE of the four is correct. This is the SECOND instance of the class the
compilationDivergesFromPaper section opens: the compilation is an LWS working
document, and its editorial additions carry no more authority than its
transcriptions do.
ACTION: the real image is attached and the description is DROPPED (splitImage
in lib.ts). Dropping is only safe BECAUSE the figure is attached — a question
with a description and no figure keeps the description, since a suspect
description beats none.
Corroboration that the readings below are right, not just different: images 1,
4 and 5 are the SAME circuit, and the 2019 / 2024 / 2025 papers do repeat this
question. Two of those three carry descriptions, and the two disagree with
each other while the drawings agree.

items.verdict: WRONG — the description brackets the parallel around S1,S2; the drawing brackets the series pair S2,S3 and puts S1 across it.

items.drawn: (S1 parallel S2) in series with S'1 in series with S'2

compilationDivergesFromPaper.compilation: If integral dx/(4x-1) = A log|4x-1| + c, then A =
compilationDivergesFromPaper.printedPaper: If integral dx/(4x-1) = A log|2x+1| + c, then A =
compilationDivergesFromPaper.finding: The compilation SILENTLY CORRECTED the board. The paper's own version is inconsistent (the integral of dx/(4x-1) is (1/4)log|4x-1|, which has nothing to do with |2x+1|), so LWS repaired the stem to make it answerable.
compilationDivergesFromPaper.consequence: The compilation is NOT a faithful transcription in every case. That matters beyond this one row: it means 'the compilation says X' is not evidence about what the board printed, and any future reconciliation against the raw papers must expect silent repairs as well as errors.
compilationDivergesFromPaper.whyItIsAmbiguous: The stem as printed admits NO value of A, so exactly one token is corrupt — and there are two equally small repairs giving DIFFERENT answers, BOTH of which are on the printed option list. (a) Fix the answer form to A log|4x-1|, giving A = 1/4 — this is the compilation's silent correction. (b) Fix the integrand to dx/(2x+1), giving A = 1/2. Nothing in the paper discriminates between them, so shipping the compilation's version does not resolve the ambiguity; it silently picks one of two coin-flip readings and presents it as the question.
compilationDivergesFromPaper.decision: RESOLVED 2026-08-12 (user's call): SHIP THE PAPER'S TEXT VERBATIM with a `[Textbook misprint: ...]` bracket that says the stem as printed has no solution, and names both repairs and both answers. Reasons: (1) these are question_kind='pyq' rows and fidelity to the printed paper is what a PYQ bank is for — a corrected PYQ is no longer a PYQ; (2) it matches settled precedent in this same corpus (the March 2022 tangent question whose given point is not on its curve, and the malformed `c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = ac`, both preserved with notes); (3) the honest note teaches more than either repair — a student who spots the inconsistency learns something, one handed a smoothed question learns nothing. Apply when the Indefinite Integration chapter is ingested in Phase 3.

boardDefects._note: Verified against the printed paper: the compilation transcribed these FAITHFULLY and the defect is the board's. Project convention is to PRESERVE a printed-paper defect and flag it honestly, never to silently repair it.

items.printed: In triangle ABC, if c^2 = a^2 + b^2 = ac, then angle B =
items.defect: A malformed double-equality that cannot hold (it forces both c^2 = ac and a^2 + b^2 = ac).
items.evidence: The 2022 paper prints exactly this. The SAME question in the 2023 paper reads 'c^2 + a^2 - b^2 = ac', which is well-formed and gives cos B = ac/(2ac) = 1/2, so B = pi/3 — option (b), matching the option list printed in 2022.
items.action: preserve + errata note naming the intended reading

items.printed: Find the equation of tangent to the curve y = 2x^3 + x^2 + 2 at (1/2, 2)
items.defect: The given point is NOT on the given curve: at x = 1/2 the curve gives 2(1/8) + 1/4 + 2 = 2.5, not 2.
items.evidence: The 2022 paper prints 'y = 2x3 + x2 + 2 at (1/2, 2)' verbatim — read from its text layer. The 2025 paper asks the same question with y = 2x^3 - x^2 + 2, which DOES pass through (1/2, 2), so the intended sign is minus.
items.action: preserve + errata note; a student answering from either reading should not be marked wrong

items.printed: Show that: integral from 0 to pi of log(1 + tan x) dx = (pi/8) log 2
items.defect: The identity is false and the integral does not even exist: tan x is undefined at pi/2, and 1 + tan x is NEGATIVE on (pi/2, 3pi/4) so the logarithm is undefined there too. The stated right-hand side (pi/8) log 2 is exactly the value over [0, pi/4], which is the classical result — so the upper limit lost its /4.
items.evidence: Maths 2022 paper.pdf page index 6, rendered at 200 dpi: the page prints the upper limit as a bare pi. Its text layer agrees and carries no '4' fragment anywhere near the integral sign. So the compilation transcribed it FAITHFULLY and the defect is the board's.
items.reversal: The authoring pass hypothesised this was OUR slip, reasoning that a board would be unlikely to misprint a limit while leaving the right-hand side exactly right for the intended one. That reasoning is sound and the conclusion was still wrong — which is the whole reason a defect report is treated as a hypothesis about WHOSE defect it is until the page is read.
items.action: preserve + errata note giving the correct limit and the correct value; do NOT repair the stem. A student who notices the integral diverges has read it correctly.

items.printed: If y = e^{m arctan x}, then show that (1 + x^2)(dy/dx)^2 + (2x - 2m) dy/dx = 0
items.defect: The identity is false. With y = e^{m arctan x} and y' = my/(1+x^2), at m = 1 and x = 0 the left-hand side is 1(1)^2 + (0 - 2)(1) = -1, not 0. Two symbols are wrong: the second derivative d^2y/dx^2 is printed as (dy/dx)^2, and m is printed as 2m. The true result, which is also the textbook's, is (1 + x^2) y_2 + (2x - m) y_1 = 0.
items.evidence: Maths 2022 paper.pdf page index 5, rendered at 200 dpi: the page prints the squared-first-derivative form and the 2m verbatim, exactly as we hold it. So the compilation is faithful and BOTH corruptions are the board's.
items.action: preserve + errata note giving the correct identity; prove the correct form in the model answer so the question is still teachable.

lostSuperscripts._finding: Four p.d.f. stems in Probability Distributions carry 'x2' where a superscript was lost. A blanket 'x2 -> x^2' rewrite would be WRONG for at least one of them, which is why they are listed individually rather than batch-fixed.

items.check: x^2/3 integrates to 1 over (-1,2) and is non-negative, so x^2 is right here. (2x/3 also integrates to 1 but goes negative on (-1,0), so it is excluded.)
x^2/32 integrates to 16/3, NOT 1 — so it is not a valid p.d.f. and 'x2 -> x^2' is wrong here. x/32 integrates to exactly 1. UNRESOLVED: the 2016 paper is scanned; settle by vision, do not assume.
same as the 2015 question — a genuine cross-year repeat; x^2/3.
x^2/18 integrates to 1 over (-3,3) and is non-negative — x^2 is right.

_finding: A stem the compilation copied WRONG, where the question still reads as a
well-formed question — which is what makes this class dangerous. Nothing
structural can catch it: the options are intact, the LaTeX is balanced, the
arithmetic is self-consistent. It surfaces only when someone SOLVES the
question and the answer comes out ugly, or contradicts a textbook twin.
All three below were found that way and then settled against the printed
page. All three are OURS, not the board's. `from` is the post-normalise
stem so extract.ts can compare by EQUALITY and refuse a near-miss.

fixes.source: Maths 2023 paper.pdf — TEXT LAYER, read directly. Item vi. of Q.1 reads 'cos^3 x dx = _______.' with no leading 1/4 anywhere.
fixes.why: The compilation prefixed a spurious \(1/4\). It is almost certainly a leaked fragment of the identity cos^3 x = (1/4)(cos 3x + 3 cos x) used to solve it. Read literally the printed-as-we-had-it stem integrates to (1/48)sin 3x + (3/16)sin x, which matches NO option — while all four options carry 1/12 on sin 3x, i.e. they were built for the unscaled integral. The option set is the evidence that the 1/4 is not part of the question.
fixes.consequence: Key A: (1/12)sin 3x + (3/4)sin x + c, which differentiates back to cos^3 x exactly.

fixes.from: Find the shortest distance between lines \(\frac{x - 1}{2} = \frac{y - 2}{2} = \frac{z - 3}{3}\) and \(\frac{x - 2}{3} = \frac{y - 4}{4} = \frac{z - 5}{5}\).
fixes.to: Find the shortest distance between lines \(\frac{x - 1}{2} = \frac{y - 2}{3} = \frac{z - 3}{4}\) and \(\frac{x - 2}{3} = \frac{y - 4}{4} = \frac{z - 5}{5}\).
fixes.source: Maths 2023 paper.pdf page index 2, rendered at 170 dpi around the 'shortest distance' hit. The page prints (x-1)/2 = (y-2)/3 = (z-3)/4.
fixes.why: The compilation gave the FIRST line the denominators 2,2,3 where the paper prints 2,3,4. The tell was the answer: as we had it the shortest distance comes out exactly 0 (the lines intersect at (-1,0,0)), and a board is very unlikely to set a 'find the shortest distance' whose answer is that the lines meet. The textbook twin carries 2,3,4 too.
fixes.consequence: With the printed direction ratios the shortest distance is 1/sqrt(6).

fixes.from: Find the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point \(P(3,2,1)\) to the line \(\overrightarrow{r} = \left( 7\widehat{i} + 7\widehat{j} + 6\widehat{k} \right) + \lambda\left( 2\widehat{i} - 2\widehat{j} + 3\widehat{k} \right)\).
fixes.to: Find the length of the perpendicular drawn from the point \(P(3,2,1)\) to the line \(\overrightarrow{r} = \left( 7\widehat{i} + 7\widehat{j} + 6\widehat{k} \right) + \lambda\left( - 2\widehat{i} + 2\widehat{j} + 3\widehat{k} \right)\).
fixes.source: Maths 2023 paper.pdf page index 3, rendered at 170 dpi around the 'length of the perpendicular' hit. The page prints lambda(-2i + 2j + 3k).
fixes.why: The compilation flipped the signs of the first TWO components of the direction vector. The tell was again the answer: as we had it the length is sqrt(953/17) = 7.49, an ugly surd, where the printed version gives exactly 7 — and the textbook twin is word-for-word identical with the printed signs.

fixes.from: If \(y = \sqrt{\sin x + \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \cdots}}}}\) \(\infty\), then show that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sec^{2}x}{2y - 1}\). Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x = 0\).
fixes.to: If \(y = \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \sqrt{\tan x + \cdots}}}}\) \(\infty\), then show that \(\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{\sec^{2}x}{2y - 1}\). Find \(\frac{dy}{dx}\) at \(x = 0\).
fixes.source: Maths 2023 paper.pdf page index 2, rendered at 200 dpi. The page prints tan x in EVERY radical, including the outermost.
fixes.why: The compilation wrote the OUTERMOST radicand as sin x while every inner one is tan x. The tell was that the identity to be shown is sec^2 x/(2y-1), which is the all-tan result: numerically at x = 0.3 the printed stem gives 0.6793 against the claimed 0.7380. A mixed-radicand nested radical is also not a thing any board would set.
fixes.consequence: All-tan. dy/dx = sec^2 x/(2y-1), and at x = 0 the convergent branch is y -> 1, giving dy/dx = 1.

fixes.from: For the following probability density function of a random variable \(X\), find (a) \(P(X < 1)\) and \(b\) \(P\left( |X| < 1 \right)\). \(f(x) = \frac{2x + 1}{18}\), for \(- 2 < x < 4\) \(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 0\), otherwise
fixes.to: For the following probability density function of a random variable \(X\), find (a) \(P(X < 1)\) and \(b\) \(P\left( |X| < 1 \right)\). \(f(x) = \frac{2x + 1}{18}\), for \(- 2 < x < 4\) \(\ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ \ = 0\), otherwise
fixes.source: Maths 2023 paper.pdf page index 2, rendered at 200 dpi. Q.25 prints f(x) = (x+2)/18 for -2 < x < 4.
fixes.why: The compilation transposed (x+2) into (2x+1). This one is nastier than most: (2x+1)/18 integrates to EXACTLY 1 over (-2,4), so it passes the obvious p.d.f. check — but it is NEGATIVE on (-2,-1/2), min -1/6, so it is not a density. The second tell is that it forces P(X<1) = 0 for a variable supported from -2.
fixes.hypothesisReversed: The authoring pass believed this was the BOARD's, on the reasoning that '2x+1' and 'x+2' are not confusable shapes for an extractor. That is true of OCR and false here: the compilation is human-typed, where a transposition is ordinary. The page settled it the other way.
fixes.consequence: f(x) = (x+2)/18 on (-2,4): integrates to 1 and is non-negative throughout. P(X<1) = 1/4, P(|X|<1) = 2/9.
